# avonet

<!-- badges: start -->
<!-- badges: end -->

[AVONET](https://figshare.com/s/b990722d72a26b5bfead) is a morphological, ecological and geographical dataset for all birds. For more information on how the dataset was compiled, please refer to [Tobias, et al. 2022](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ele.13898).

The goal of the `avonet` package is to give users access to AVONET data comfortably from within an R session. It queries a Postgres database directly, so there are no flat files to download or keep in sync: you connect once, then pull traits for any taxon, filter them, and get the literature sources needed to cite them back alongside the data.

## Installation

You can install the development version of `avonet` from [GitHub](https://github.com/) with:

``` r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("kfrac/avonet")
```

No database credentials? The package bundles a snapshot of two taxa and runs
without a connection — see [Working without a
connection](#working-without-a-connection) at the end.

## Connecting

Connecting to the AVONET database is as easy as entering your username and password. We recommend using the `keyring` package to manage your credentials.

```{r DB_connection}
library(avonet)
library(keyring)
db_user <- key_list("avonet")[1, "username"]
db_password <- key_get("avonet", username = db_user)
connect_db(username = db_user, pw = db_password)
```

Every function below assumes an open connection to the database. AVONET carries three parallel taxonomies and every query must provide one: BirdLife (`1`), eBird (`2`) or BirdTree (`3`).

## Two kinds of data

AVONET holds trait data at two resolutions, and the difference shapes every query.

**Species-level** traits — habitat, trophic niche, mass, range size and the rest — are recorded once per species, so a query returns one row per species.

**Specimen-level** morphology — beak, wing, tarsus and tail measurements — is recorded per individual bird that was measured, so a species may have one row or dozens. These measurements are what distinguishes AVONET from a species checklist: they carry the within-species variation that a single published mean throws away, and each one comes with the sex, life stage, country and source of the bird it was taken from.

`get_traits()` returns both. The species-level traits come back in `data`, one row per species; the measurements come back separately in `specimen_data`, one row per specimen. Keeping them apart avoids repeating every species-level value across each specimen of that species. Pass `resolution = "species"` to skip the specimen query when you do not need it.

## Getting your bearings

Traits are organized into groups, and each group can be listed with its descriptions, possible values and primary source.

```{r trait_groups}
get_trait_groups()
```

```{r trait_list}
get_trait_list(group = "eco")
```

For a categorical trait, the valid levels can be pulled directly — useful for building a filter without guessing at spelling.

```{r trait_levels}
get_trait_levels("habitat")
```

Passing `return_defs = TRUE` returns what each level actually means, rather than just its name.

```{r trait_level_defs}
get_trait_levels("trophic_niche", return_defs = TRUE)
```

## Querying traits

`get_traits()` is the single entry point for trait data. It accepts names at any rank — species, genus, family or order — and works out which is which, so one call can mix them.

```{r traits_basic}
buteo <- get_traits("Buteo", taxonomy = 1)
names(buteo)
```

The result is a list: `data` holds one row per species, `specimen_data` holds the individual measurements behind those species, `metadata_summary` describes each trait and where it came from, and `detailed_sources` holds the full literature references behind those sources — so a result can be cited without a second lookup.

```{r traits_data}
buteo$data[, c("species", "family", "habitat", "trophic_niche", "mass_value")]
```

```{r traits_metadata}
head(buteo$metadata_summary, 4)
```

Taxonomic ranks are detected per name, and reported, so you can see how an ambiguous name was read. Here `resolution = "species"` keeps the call to the species-level traits alone.

```{r traits_rank}
hawks <- get_traits("Accipitridae", taxonomy = 1, resolution = "species")
nrow(hawks$data)
```

Each trait carries a source. These are stripped from `data` by default, since the same information is summarized in `metadata_summary`, but `source_cols = TRUE` keeps them inline.

```{r example_source_cols, message = FALSE}
names(get_traits("Buteo buteo", taxonomy = 1, source_cols = TRUE)$data)
```

## Filtering

Filters are a named list, applied to the data after it returns. Categorical traits take a value or a set of values; numeric traits take an operator and a value. Conditions combine with AND.

```{r traits_filter, message = FALSE}
forest_hawks <- get_traits(
  "Accipitridae",
  taxonomy = 1,
  filter = list(habitat    = "Forest",
                range_size = list(op = "<", val = 5000000))
)

head(forest_hawks$data[, c("species", "habitat", "range_size", "mass_value")])
```

Filtering on a column that was not queried is an error rather than an empty result, and the message lists what is available. Specimens are fetched only for the species that survive the filter, so `specimen_data` always matches what ended up in `data`.

## Working with the measurements

`specimen_data` holds one row per measured bird, with the species it belongs to in the first column.

```{r traits_specimen, message = FALSE}
specimens <- get_traits("Buteo buteo", taxonomy = 1)
head(specimens$specimen_data)
```

Supplying `aggregate` collapses those measurements into per-species means and counts for a given grouping — `"sex"`, `"life stage"`, `"country"`, `"source type"` or `"all"`. Grouping is always by species first, so a call covering several species never pools their measurements together.

```{r traits_aggregate, message = FALSE}
by_sex <- get_traits("Buteo buteo", taxonomy = 1, aggregate = "sex")

by_sex$specimen_data
```

## Checking a name before querying

Taxonomies disagree, and names get split, merged and renamed. `get_taxonomic_info()` shows what a search term resolves to, and how it matched.

```{r taxonomic_info}
get_taxonomic_info(search_term = "Buteo buteo", taxonomy = 1)
```

```{r taxonomic_info_rank}
head(get_taxonomic_info(search_term = "Buteo", taxonomy = 1))
```

## Disconnecting

Remember to disconnect from the database at the end!

```{r DB_disconnect}
disconnect_db()
```

## Working without a connection

The package bundles a snapshot of two taxa — the order Accipitriformes and the
family Sylviidae — across every taxonomy that carries them. Everything works
against it with no database at all, which is what makes these examples
reproducible and lets you try the package before asking for credentials.

The connection was closed in the section above, and yet:

```{r example_data}
hawks <- get_traits("Accipitriformes", taxonomy = 1)
nrow(hawks$data)
nrow(hawks$specimen_data)
```

```{r example_data_taxonomy}
head(get_taxonomic_info("Sylviidae", taxonomy = 1))
```

There is nothing to switch on. With no usable connection the package reads the
bundled data and says so; with one it reads the database. `connect_db()` is the
only thing that changes which, so a snapshot can never shadow live data.

Both taxa are bundled complete, so any species, genus or family at or below
them is a faithful answer, and a taxon with nothing bundled returns no rows
just as an unknown one would against the database. A taxon *wider* than
either — the order Passeriformes, say, which contains Sylviidae — returns only
the bundled part of itself and warns that it has. `get_trait_list()` describes
only the bundled subset while this is in force.

Coverage is uneven across taxonomies, since the names themselves differ:
BirdLife has 252 Accipitriformes and 69 Sylviidae, eBird 252 and none (it
carries no Sylviidae family label at all), BirdTree 251 and 294.
